editorNote: Info ’83 shows the personal computer growing into an office workstation, while Coleco brings its ambitious Adam bundle into the holiday home-computer battle.
morningLine: Networks link the desks, Adam reaches the shops, and a new generation of computer games fills the shelf.

lead.headline: Info ’83 Turns the Personal Computer Into an Office Workstation
lead.dek: DEC combines word processing, personal computing and communications as software and small networks dominate the New York exposition.
body: Software announcements dominated the 10th International Information Management Exposition & Conference in New York, but the larger story was integration. Machines once sold as dedicated word processors were being recast as connected personal workstations, able to prepare documents, exchange files and reach an office network from the same desk.

Digital Equipment Corporation’s Decmate Office Workstation made that convergence explicit. Its $4,735 package included the system unit, monitor, keyboard, Easycom logon software and WPS Convert, tying word processing to personal-computing and communications tasks under a 90-day on-site service plan.

The network followed the workstation onto the show floor. General Binding’s Northnet linked System 9 desktop micros, printers and disks for $4,400 per workstation, with electronic mail available as an option. Wordplex’s $450-per-node Wordlink could connect as many as 16 RS-232C electronic typewriters to shared printers while documents continued to arrive.

Software also promised a friendlier conversation with large machines. Frey Associates showed Themis, a VAX-11 information system that accepted plain-English queries from a base vocabulary exceeding 900 words and could learn more. Info ’83’s crowded aisles offered a clear forecast: office computing would be connected, software-led and increasingly personal.

stories.headline: Coleco’s $700 Adam Enters the Holiday Computer Fight
stories.dek: A printer, tape drive and 64K system arrive as one ambitious family bundle.
body: With federal approval secured in late September, Coleco expected Adam systems to reach stores in October. Priced around $700, the much-advertised package joined a bruising home-computer market with 64K of memory, a Digital Data Pack tape drive, keyboard, daisy-wheel printer and productivity software.

Adam’s complete-computer configuration also carried ColecoVision compatibility, giving console households an expansion story as well as a new machine. The unusual design made the printer the computer’s power supply, so Coleco’s headline bundle was inseparable in practice—a bold value pitch carrying equally bold engineering risk.

stories.headline: Desktop Networks and Electronic Mail Move Downmarket
stories.dek: Small systems share files and printers without waiting for the mainframe.
body: Northnet placed a server station over a cable network of System 9 desktop computers and peripherals, while leaving stations able to make independent connections. Its 16-bit node doubled as a file server, bringing the vocabulary of networking to modest office machines.

Wordlink aimed at another installed base: electronic typewriters. Up to 16 RS-232C machines could receive documents and share printers at $450 per node. Together the systems made electronic mail and shared resources practical product features rather than distant promises.

stories.headline: Portable and Multiuser Micros Crowd the Show
stories.dek: Suitcase systems meet Unix and MP/M-86 multiuser desktops.
body: Manufacturers unveiled desktop and portable systems at Info ’83 even as much of the microcomputer trade held its announcements for November’s Comdex. Xerox had introduced a portable days earlier, evidence that transportable IBM-compatible computing was becoming a recognized category.

At the other end of the range, Philips showed a 32-bit multiuser supermicro compatible with Unix and its workstation line. A Rair MP/M-86 desktop supported as many as 16 terminals and peripherals, included 1MB of memory and listed for $9,750; Computer Transceiver offered a dual-processor system for $3,295.
